title: Composio vs. Pipedream vs. Nango: Connecting Agents to Existing Accounts
summary: Choose agent integrations by authorization, prebuilt actions, custom functions, synchronization, and the maintenance your product needs to own.
body_markdown:
Composio, Pipedream Connect, and Nango can all reduce the work involved in connecting an agent to existing customer accounts. The decision turns on how you want to discover actions, manage authorization, implement integration logic, and keep external data current.


Start with the integration your product must own. Reading a document once, keeping a CRM synchronized, and letting an agent choose among business actions create different runtime and maintenance requirements. A useful comparison makes those differences explicit before counting connectors.


**Reviewed October 18, 2026. Disclosure:** o11 publishes this article and offers adjacent tool infrastructure. This review uses current official documentation, not paid hands-on tests. Capability descriptions establish documented product scope; they do not establish performance, account eligibility, or suitability for every provider.


## Define the integration you need


An application integration has at least four parts. First, a user connects the correct external account. Second, your application or agent performs a supported operation. Third, you maintain the connection and any data over time. Fourth, you govern access when users, workspaces, or permissions change.


These parts have different failure modes. A stale token blocks the first. A provider-specific required field complicates the second. Missed updates undermine the third. An incorrect tenant mapping breaks the fourth, even when every network request succeeds.


Write one concrete workflow before evaluating products. For example: a customer connects a CRM, your service imports selected accounts, an agent enriches a chosen record, and a reviewed action writes the proposed update. Include deletion and disconnection behavior in the same specification.


The important phrase is selected accounts. Integration products cannot decide your application’s business permissions automatically. You still need a trustworthy mapping between your authenticated user, workspace, external connection, and allowed action. Our[provider credential guide](https://o11.ai/blog/agent-provider-credentials) explains the application-side ownership decisions that remain after adopting managed infrastructure.


## The documented platform models


Composio’s developer documentation organizes agent access around sessions, toolkits, authentication, and execution, with MCP and framework paths. This makes it relevant when a model needs to discover and perform operations across connected apps. Evaluate which tools the session exposes for a specific end user and how connection requirements are surfaced.[Composio documentation](https://docs.composio.dev/docs) .


Pipedream Connect documents managed user authorization, prebuilt actions and triggers, an MCP server, custom requests through a proxy, and multi-step workflows. Its model is useful to assess when your product needs both ready-made actions and programmable integration paths.[Pipedream Connect overview](https://pipedream.com/docs/connect) .


Nango’s current introduction describes Auth and Functions as its core primitives. Users connect accounts; developers control TypeScript integration functions for actions, synchronization, and webhooks; selected actions can be exposed to agents through schemas and MCP. This is broader than simply storing OAuth tokens.[Nango introduction](https://nango.dev/docs/getting-started/intro-to-nango) .


## Compare the responsibilities


Responsibility Composio evaluation Pipedream Connect evaluation Nango evaluation


Agent chooses an action Session discovery and exact tool schemas MCP or selected prebuilt actions Selected action functions and exposed schemas


User connects an account Auth configuration and user-specific connection Connect authorization and end-user identity Auth configuration and connection mapping


Custom integration behavior Extension path and provider-specific execution Custom requests, components, or workflows Developer-controlled functions


Ongoing data movement Verify requirements for your data lifecycle Triggers and workflow behavior for the exact app Sync and webhook function behavior


Production ownership Identity, policy, observability, recovery Same requirements Same requirements


This is an evaluation map rather than a universal ranking. An integration that takes an hour with a suitable prebuilt action might take substantially longer if a missing provider field requires custom work. Conversely, custom code can be the right investment when the integration is a core product feature.


Ask each vendor for the smallest complete implementation of your workflow. A generic demonstration of logging into an app does not show incremental data synchronization, and a synchronization demo does not show an agent choosing safe write actions.


## Authorization affects onboarding


A connection flow needs to preserve context. When the user returns from an external consent screen, your backend must know the intended application user, workspace, provider, and requested permissions. It must also handle cancellation and partial failure without claiming that access is ready.


Pipedream’s managed-auth quickstart provides a concrete connect-token and end-user setup path. Inspect those identifiers as security-relevant application data: an arbitrary identifier supplied by the browser should not let a user impersonate another customer’s connection.[Pipedream managed-auth quickstart](https://pipedream.com/docs/connect/managed-auth/quickstart) .


For all three products, test a user who belongs to two workspaces and has two accounts with the same provider. Let them disconnect one and reconnect another. Confirm that old jobs do not silently acquire the replacement account, and that the UI can explain which account a tool will use.


Token refresh is another separate case. Managed refresh can reduce maintenance work, but your application still needs to present expired or revoked access clearly. A retry policy should not repeatedly send the user through a broken consent flow or substitute an unrelated identity to avoid an error.


## Prebuilt actions versus code-owned logic


Prebuilt actions are attractive when the provider operation closely matches your product requirement. The developer avoids hand-writing request construction, credential handling, and some response interpretation. The benefit compounds when a prototype spans several APIs.


The limitation appears when your product needs a provider-specific option that the action does not expose, a custom transformation, or a composite operation. Evaluate the escape hatch before you need it. Can you add a field, call the underlying API, or define a custom action while retaining the managed connection?


Code-owned integration logic offers explicit control over behavior and review. It also creates a maintenance obligation. Your team must understand the provider’s pagination, data model, and side effects, even if infrastructure handles execution and credentials.


Do not frame this as automation versus control. Decide which behavior is commodity and which is part of your product’s differentiation. A prebuilt record lookup can be sufficient, while your own logic determines how conflicting customer data is reconciled. Keep those responsibilities separate so you can update one without rewriting the other.


## Syncs and tool calls have different contracts


A tool call usually answers a bounded request. A sync maintains a changing collection over time. Treating the latter as a loop around the former can produce missed updates, duplicates, and expensive full reimports.


For a sync, define the cursor, deletion semantics, checkpoint, backfill behavior, and recovery after a provider outage. Ask whether updates are delivered once, at least once, or under another documented contract. Your consumer should be prepared for duplicate notifications whenever the delivery model permits them.


For an action, define the intended side effect and how you know it completed. A timeout after a create request is different from a validation rejection before it was sent. Retrying both identically can create duplicate records.


Nango’s documented function model explicitly includes actions, syncs, and webhooks; Pipedream documents triggers and workflows; Composio documents triggers alongside tools. These labels help locate the relevant feature, but the exact provider operation and lifecycle still need verification. Keep a responsibility matrix that identifies which layer owns checkpoints, retries, and reconciliation for your proposed integration.


## Schemas determine agent usability


An operation that works from application code may still be difficult for a model to use. The code author may know that an account ID differs from a company ID or that a field expects an internal enum. The model needs that information in the tool contract or a discoverable instruction.


Evaluate representative tasks without quietly giving one platform extra hints. Record whether the agent chooses the right action, produces valid arguments, and interprets the response correctly. Include tasks where the correct answer is to ask for missing information or stop.


Scope the tool set to what the task needs. A narrow selection reduces accidental writes and makes discovery less ambiguous. That does not require deleting the broader catalog; it means exposing capabilities deliberately for a particular agent role.


The[schema usability experiment](https://o11.ai/blog/test-agent-tool-schema-usability) provides a repeatable way to separate tool selection, argument construction, and outcome quality. Use it to improve your integration rather than assume that adding MCP automatically makes every provider action understandable.


## Cost the integration over time


Pricing units can differ across connected-user counts, executions, workflows, compute time, or support arrangements. Read the current plan for your expected deployment and include the provider’s own bill. Managed authorization does not remove the customer’s commercial relationship with its CRM or document service.


Use an illustrative planning equation: monthly integration cost equals platform commitments plus metered execution plus supplier charges plus maintenance effort. Keep cash and engineering effort separate in the report, even if you also convert engineering hours into a planning estimate.


Estimate three cases: a low-usage prototype, the expected production workload, and a growth case with more connected customers. Include customers who connect an account but use it rarely. A low per-execution figure can obscure a different charge that grows with customer count.


Then consider maintenance events. How much work does a provider schema change create? Can you inspect failures without exposing customer secrets? Who handles expired authorizations? The[hidden cost of adding another API](https://o11.ai/blog/hidden-api-setup-cost) describes the engineering work that a purely runtime price comparison misses.


## Run a complete lifecycle pilot


Use an isolated test workspace with data you are authorized to access. Connect one account, read a small collection, perform a reversible approved action, and verify the result directly. Then disconnect the account and confirm that future access stops.


Exercise one provider rate limit, one malformed input, and one interruption after dispatch using a documented sandbox or local fixture. Record what your application receives and what recovery requires. A platform that makes these states clear can save more engineering time than one that only makes the happy path shorter.


For ongoing syncs, change and delete a record while the integration is temporarily paused. Resume it and verify the final state. This detects whether the proposed design can recover from missed events rather than merely process a demonstration webhook.


Keep the pilot evidence: configuration version, provider scopes, timestamps, request identifiers, expected records, actual outcomes, and remaining questions. Avoid storing access tokens in the artifact. These records become the basis for a defensible buying decision and an onboarding runbook for your team.


## Choose the platform that fits your ownership model


Shortlist Composio when agent discovery and execution across connected apps are central. Shortlist Pipedream Connect when its combination of managed authorization, prebuilt actions, custom requests, and workflows fits the product. Shortlist Nango when developer-controlled integration functions and ongoing data synchronization match the responsibilities you want to own.


Verify each conclusion against your exact workflow. These are starting points based on documented product models, not universal boundaries or a claim that alternatives cannot support adjacent use cases.


If the remaining gap is access to occasional paid research or media services, evaluate that separately from customer-account integration. A shared paid-tool layer can complement connected business accounts. The architectural win is fewer repeated setup and maintenance tasks, while keeping identity, data ownership, and execution behavior explicit.
